*Chao*: As for the Dharma of Prajñā, it is precisely the Dharma of the True Suchness Mind-Seal (*tathatā-cittamudrā*). Now, as for this Dharma of the Mind-Seal, it is neither form nor emptiness;
its delusive appearances are fundamentally exhausted, and its true nature is fundamentally manifest. Therefore, this Dharma of True Suchness, from the very beginning...
It comes to be free from the marks of verbal expression, free from the marks of names and words, and free from the marks of mental objects.
It is ultimately equal, without change or variation, and indestructible; it is solely this one mind, and is therefore called True Suchness (Tathatā). △ Third, the citation of scriptural proof.
The text below states: "To be free from all marks is precisely what is called 'all Buddhas. It further says: "The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.
This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real."
△ Sixth, for the sake of those with the most superior faculties. This is divided into three parts. First, the heading:
"Sixth, for the sake of those with the most superior faculties of the One Vehicle.
△ Second, the explanation.
This refers to the Dharma of Prajñā. Originally, it is not something that can be sustained by those of inferior faculties (*indriya*).
[Commentary: There are three types of faculties and five natures (*gotra*) of capacity. That which is now being bestowed is the Supreme Vehicle;

thus, none but those with the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) can enter it. Question: It is only when the three faculties are universally moistened and both the Great and Small Vehicles are simultaneously embraced that this Dharma may be established.
This is merely its perfect subtlety. Why is it that it reaches only those of great capacity (*mahā-yāna*) and not those of small capacity (*hīna-yāna*)? Answer:
Did we not say previously that all Mahāyāna sūtras and the teachings of the Three Vehicles take the true mark (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) as their foundation?
That it does not reach the small [vehicle] but reaches the great has three meanings: first, to lead those who have not yet resolved to attain the Great Mind.

First, it is to cause them to generate the Great Mind (mahācitta). Second, for those who have already generated the Great Mind, it is to cause them to dwell forever in the state of non-retrogression (avaivartika).
Third, it is to cause those of the two vehicles (dvayayāna) to give rise to great shame and remorse, thereby entering the Buddha-wisdom (buddhajñāna).

For these reasons, it is said that the Tathāgata speaks of "generating the Mahāyāna," and so forth. By means of this skillful speech, he causes those of the Small Vehicle (hīnayāna) to develop deep faith in the Mahāyāna. II.

The True Suchness of Emptiness. Furthermore, advancing to exhaust the heights of the tower, they turn their minds toward the Great [Vehicle]. It is not that they truly reject it but fail to receive it.
△ Third, citing scriptural evidence, divided into two parts. First, being received solely by those of superior capacity.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The Tathāgata speaks for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna; he speaks for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.
Second, stimulating and drawing in those of inferior capacity:

it further states, "If there are those who delight in the Lesser Dharma, who are attached to the notions of self, person, and so forth, they will be unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain [it] to others."

Commentary: "Bearing the burden of the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*" means that those who delight in inferior teachings (*hīna-dharma*) take pleasure only in the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), yet do not understand the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Because they do not know that there are no phenomena outside the mind, they fail to realize that the five aggregates (*skandha*), six sense bases (*āyatana*), twelve spheres (*āyatana*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are fundamentally empty and quiescent, and are devoid of self (*anātman*).
There is no person, no sentient being, and no life-span possessor.

Because they have not yet been liberated from the attachment to dharmas and views, they are unable to hear, unable to receive and uphold, unable to read and recite, and furthermore, unable to benefit others by explaining and analyzing [the teachings] for them, nor able to shoulder the unsurpassed Great Bodhi.
△ Seven: To demonstrate that seeing one's nature must involve cultivation, divided into three parts.
First, the heading.
Seven reasons why one must practice in order to realize the nature.
△ Second, the explanation.

That is to say, if one does not maintain ethical discipline and cultivate merit, then even if one upholds, recites, and studies these scriptural passages, there will ultimately be no benefit—just like the case of a painted cake used to satisfy hunger.
Conversely, it is essential to maintain ethical discipline and cultivate merit regarding these scriptural passages.
One can give rise to the mind of faith, which immediately gives rise to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Commentary: Now, cultivation and realization are certainly not non-existent, yet defilement must not be permitted. Therefore, when the Great Matter is not yet clarified, it is as if one has lost one’s parents;
once the Great Matter is clarified, one must still regard it as if one had lost one’s parents. Thus, we know that after the nature of seeing has been realized, one must necessarily...
One realizes it through provisional cultivation. If one does not practice, how could the ignorance of kalpas be severed? Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:

"Even if one upholds, receives, reads, and recites [the teachings], if one does not sever killing, stealing, lust, and lying, it is like steaming sand to make rice—it will certainly yield no real fruit.
Furthermore, the Elder Lianchi said: "What benefit does a painted cake provide for a hungry stomach?"
False jade cannot deceive the true value of a gem. Therefore, it is essential that concentration arises from precepts, and wisdom is brought forth by concentration;

these constitute the Tathāgata’s three untainted trainings (trīṇi śaikṣāṇi anāsravāṇi). This is a definitive and pure instruction. Thus it is said: "It is essential to uphold the precepts and cultivate merit.
If one can give rise to faith in these words and phrases, one will immediately give rise to the reality-mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). As for the upholder of precepts, the precepts...
Cultivating merit is concentration (*samādhi*). Giving rise to faith is wisdom (*prajñā*). These constitute the foundation for all stages.
"Giving rise to the true aspect" means giving rise to the true aspect of the various stages; that is to say, by severing the ten obstacles and realizing the ten suchnesses.
△ Third, citing scriptural evidence.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "By means of no-self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span, one cultivates all wholesome dharmas;
thus one immediately attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Commentary: From "Because there is no self or person" onwards is the section on the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). "Cultivating all wholesome dharmas" is the section on the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
"Thereby attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" is the section on the Path of Realization (*adhigamamārga*). △ Eighth, showing that complete cultivation is itself the nature (*dharmatā*);
this is divided into three parts. First, the heading.
Eighth, it is for the purpose of causing them to know that the complete cultivation [of all practices] is itself the nature [of reality].
△ Second, the explanation:
This means to cause all bodhisattvas to thoroughly understand that the myriad practices of the six perfections are none other than the wondrous practice of *prajñā*, by means of one...
All gates of practice are the complete cultivation that is identical to nature, because there is no duality in their practice.
The *Commentary* states: "Complete cultivation is identical to nature" refers to the Dharma of the Single Practice Samādhi of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
By the power of the Single Practice Samādhi of True Suchness, one enters immeasurable gates of samādhi; therefore, one attains the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
This is precisely the one mind. By awakening to the myriad practices as being of one essence, it is said that "there is no duality of dharmas. △ Third, the citation of proof:
The following text states: "If there are those who resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should give rise to this thought: 'I ought to extinguish...'"
He delivers all sentient beings. Having delivered all sentient beings, yet there is not a single sentient being who has been truly delivered.
Because he penetrates the practice of the Dharma through non-self, the Tathāgata calls him a true Bodhisattva.
Commentary: Having realized one's own nature, one understands that the living being and the Buddha are as one; that both oneself and sentient beings are originally quiescent and extinguished.
How, then, could there be a "self" that can deliver sentient beings, or a "self" that can practice? Therefore, it is said: "One who has attained mastery in the practice of non-self."
Only now do we know that complete cultivation is itself the nature; thus the Tathāgata names such a person a "True Mahāsattva.
△ Ninth, showing the elimination of heavy obstructions, divided into three parts. First, the heading:
Ninth, it is for the sake of causing Bodhisattvas with many obstructions to eliminate their heavy obstructions.
△ Second, the explanation:
This means that even if a bodhisattva has generated the great resolve and passed through many accumulated kalpas, heavy obstacles may still be difficult to eliminate.

Therefore, they are caused to uphold the Prajñāpāramitā dharma so that heavy obstacles are transformed into light ones, thereby destroying both the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

The Commentary states: Although one has generated the Great Mind, if ordinary afflictions have not been severed and the Prajñā has not yet been tasted, then even after practicing the perfection of giving and other paramitas for many kalpas, one will not transcend the birth-and-death of the triple world with its limited segments, nor will one attain the eradication of active afflictions and all heavy obstacles;
therefore, it is urged that through the power of reciting the Mahayana Prajñā, these [obstacles] shall finally be dissolved.

Because these are the most severe afflictions and karmic obstacles of retribution, the Chapter on Samantabhadra states: "If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true nature of reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, with a sincere mind, repent for the emotions of the six sense faculties, and then recite the meaning of the Mahāyāna."

This is because heavy hindrances are transformed into light hindrances. "Heavy hindrances" refer to afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the hindrance of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
"Light hindrances" refer to the hindrance to the known (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

By the power of upholding Prajñā, one first destroys the two types of conceptual grasping and the manifest afflictions, and subsequently destroys the hindrance to the known—namely, the Prajñā of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
The power is strong; there are no innate latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are not severed. △ Third, the citation of proof:

The text below states, "If this person’s karmic offenses from previous lives should have caused them to fall into the evil realms, by virtue of being slighted and despised by people in the present life, their karmic offenses from previous lives are immediately extinguished, and they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Commentary: "Those with karmic offenses from previous lives" refers to karma combined with the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). "Falling into evil realms" refers to the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
By virtue of upholding the inherent power of Prajñāpāramitā, one eliminates the causal seeds of offenses from former lives and extinguishes the obstacle of retribution for the future.

Consequently, one undergoes contempt and disdain from worldly people; thus, heavy karma is avoided and transformed into light reception, while heavy retribution is dissolved and transformed into light retribution.

Therefore, the *Sūtra on Purifying Karmic Obstructions* states: "If there is a bodhisattva who has committed all manner of offenses in previous lives, and although the causes and effects have not yet ripened, they fear receiving the retribution in the future;

or if, in the present life, while practicing according to the teachings and reciting the Mahāyāna sūtras, they instead suffer from a grave illness that is difficult to endure or bear, or even encounter calamities lasting for as long as a single day and night—they are able to..."

It extinguishes the Avīci Hell and all grave offenses; how much more so after many days? One shall surely attain the lower [stages], for this is precisely when the two obstacles are severed and the two fruits are realized.
△ Tenth, Severing Doubt and Generating Faith. This section has three parts. First, the heading.
Tenth, it is for the purpose of severing both the active manifestations and the seeds of all doubts regarding *prajñā*.
△ Second, the explanation, which is divided into three parts. First, entering through faith.
This refers to doubt: doubt acts as an obstacle to the gateway of the myriad virtues, whereas being free from doubt serves as the progress for faith to achieve *bodhi*. Therefore, one is able to—
One enters samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, thereby realizing the sublime Dharma gates such as the Prajñāpāramitā.
The *Huayan* states: "Faith is the root of unsurpassed bodhi; faith enables one to surely reach the stage of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, within the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma, faith is that which enables entry. Thus, we know that doubt is a major obstacle to the Holy Path; by being free from doubt, one is liberated.

There are eight indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), namely: regret, sleep, vitarka, vicāra, greed, hatred, pride, and doubt. These comprise the six aforementioned categories.

There are forty-six [factors]. Regarding the four [categories], the fourteen factors of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are: first, acquisition (*prāpti*); second, non-acquisition (*aprāpti*); third, homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*); fourth, the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*);

fifth, the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); sixth, the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); seventh, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); eighth, birth (*jāti*); ninth, subsistence (*sthiti*);
tenth, change (*jarā*); eleventh, aging (*anityatā*); twelfth, name (*nāman*); thirteenth, phrase (*pada*); and fourteenth, phoneme (*vyañjana*). Therefore, the verse says: "Acquisition..."

Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), life-force (*jīvita*), as well as birth, duration, change, and cessation (*jarā-anityatā*), along with the sets of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*)—these five categories, together with the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena:
first, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); second, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
and third, space (*ākāśa*)—constitute the seventy-five phenomena in total. Within this Mahāyāna [system], twenty-five of these are lacking; they shall be discussed below.

[Explanation: Although the number is not explicitly stated in the current text, its meaning is implicitly contained within it. What is taught below concerns only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Following this, the second section clarifies the distinction between the two types of emptiness. This is because followers of the Two Vehicles possess inferior faculties and are thus not yet capable of hearing the teaching on the true principle of the two emptinesses.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 31, states: "The disciples of the Hīnayāna have dull faculties; therefore, for their sake..."

Various teachings speak of the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). The *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states: "Regarding those with the view of a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*), because the faculties of the two vehicles are pure, the Tathāgata taught them only the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and so forth;

even when he spoke of the two kinds of emptiness, it was for the most part not clearly revealed. This is because [the two vehicles] rely on the six consciousnesses and the three poisons to establish their path.
Below this, the third section clarifies the fundamental basis upon which they rely. However, the Lesser Vehicle calculates the root of birth and death as follows:

Although there are many types of fundamental [causes], I shall briefly cite three of them. First, the calculation of consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*), as explained in the eighth fascicle of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* regarding the Sautrāntika masters:
they take present form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) as the causes of defilement and purity.

This means that, just as in the Mahāyāna, the eighth [consciousness] serves as the object of perfuming (*bhāvyatva*). Second, the meaning of the three poisons as the cause, as clarified in the Mahāyāna.
Because the preceding seven consciousnesses act as the perfuming agents (*vāsaka*), they cause the *āgama* to be cited; however, this merely serves to establish the three poisons.

As for the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), it means that by taking the three poisons as causes and conditions, the three types of karma (*trividha-karman*) arise; and by the causes and conditions of the three types of karma, the three realms (*traidhātuka*) arise.
Therefore, among all phenomena, the chapter on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) states: "Sentient beings are deluded..."
It is that which is covered. It gives rise to the three types of conduct for the future. Because these conducts exist, consciousness receives bodies within the six realms;

this is precisely the meaning. Thirdly, taking the two meanings mentioned above, both possess the capacity to be perfumed and the capacity to perfume, for it is through perfuming that there is cyclic flow (*saṃsāra*).
If this is so, how does this differ from the Mahāyāna? Nevertheless, the reason it differs from the intent of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* is simply that [the latter] speaks of only six...

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not the eighth [consciousness] that serves as the perfumable (*bhāvya*); even if one speaks of the *ālayavijñāna*, it exists only as a name. Furthermore, the perfuming agent (*bhāvaka*) is not the seven consciousnesses;

therefore, they are entirely different. Fourth, "because the source of phenomena has not been fully exhausted" means that among unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), there are only three types—cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), and space (*ākāśa*)—and true suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth do not yet exist.

This is for the purpose of clarifying the two kinds of emptiness; it is simply because [this teaching] has not yet exhausted the source of all phenomena. △ Second, the explanation of the Initial Teaching (Śākyadeśanā).
The text is divided into two parts: first, the enumeration of names;
second, the Mahāyāna Initial Teaching.
Commentary: "Great" (mahā) has the meaning of distinguishing from the "small. "Vehicle" (yāna) has the meaning of conveying or transporting.

Because the teachings of the aforementioned Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) could only benefit oneself, whereas in this Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) one universally transports all beings, it is called "Great. As for "beginning":
Because this teaching within the present dispensation concerns what has not yet been exhausted, whereas previous teachings concerned what was already exhausted, it is called "the beginning" (*ādi*).
△ Second, the explanation of the text, in two parts: first, the explanation of the name and its meaning.
Because the second period clarified only emptiness, and the third period taught the three vehicles while not permitting that those of fixed nature (icchantikas) could attain Buddhahood—
thus failing to exhaustively present the ultimate teaching of the Mahāyāna— it is called "initial. Furthermore, because it posits both those who attain Buddhahood and those who do not,
it is also called "partial."

Commentary: Regarding the statement that "in the second period, only emptiness was clarified," this follows the judgment of the master Jñānaprabha concerning the temporal sequence of the Buddha’s teachings throughout his lifetime.

Because the first period—the Hīnayāna teachings—clarified that both the objective realm and the subjective mind exist, the second period taught the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* Mahāyāna for those of middling faculties.
In this teaching, the objective realm is empty while the mind exists, thereby revealing the principle of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only), as those of middling faculties...
It was still inferior, as it had not yet fully entered into the equality of true emptiness. Therefore, the present commentary states: "In the second period, only emptiness was clarified;
in the third period, for those of the highest faculties, the signless Mahāyāna was taught, distinguishing that both mind and objects are empty."

Because they are equal and of one taste. The commentary’s statement that "the third period teaches the three vehicles and does not permit [others]" is not the meaning of the master Jñānaprabha regarding the third period;
rather, it simply adopts the view of the master Śīlabhadra based on the intent of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.

First, in the Hīnayāna it is taught that only the Buddha alone possesses the nature of great awakening, while for others it is not said to exist; therefore, [the former position] is entirely untenable.
Next, "certainly established" refers to the second period, when only the One Vehicle was taught, wherein all sentient beings are able to attain Buddhahood;
this is what is meant by "certainly established. If everyone were to attain it, it would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); if no one were to attain it, it would be...

This is far from being excessive; therefore, all [teachings] are skillful means and are equally incomplete. This is because, at the first stage, since [beings] were not yet capable of hearing the Great [Vehicle], there was a one-sided suppression [of their potential].

At the second stage, they were encouraged to aspire toward Buddhahood, which was a one-sided exaltation. During the third stage, the three vehicles were taught according to the principle as a correct exposition:
those with the nature [to attain Buddhahood] will all achieve it, while those without that nature will not. Thus, it is not overly extreme.

Therefore, it is called "accomplished" (*niṣpanna*), because it universally brings forth all vehicles. This is according to the intent of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, which is an expedient teaching (*neyārtha*).
Why is this so? Within the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, the second turning of the wheel is described as "allowing all sentient beings to attain Buddhahood";

this is the ultimate, definitive teaching (*nītārtha*) of the supreme One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. How, then, could one rely upon the [teachings of the] *Saṃdhinirmocana* [to negate that]?
The phrase "the second period" implicitly refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as being of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). Therefore, Qingliang said:
"Who has judged the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to be of provisional meaning? Furthermore, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:
"Those of the śrāvaka lineage who are intent on quiescence, though they receive the edification of all Buddhas, ultimately cannot attain unexcelled bodhi. All of these [passages]...
It is definitively not permitted that those of the two vehicles with fixed natures, nor those of no-nature such as the Icchantikas, can attain Buddhahood; how then could this be a literal teaching?

Therefore, it is said that this has not yet exhausted the ultimate discourse of the Mahāyāna. Consequently, we now adopt the interpretation of the Master Jñānaprabha regarding the second period of the wheel of Dharma:
namely, that objects are empty while mind exists, which is the Dharmalakṣaṇa-Mahāyāna, based on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. Regarding the third...
Regarding the doctrine of the three periods of teaching: now, the Great Master Xianshou synthesizes the entirety of the One Teaching.

Since this is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna, yet it is not yet fully realized, it is established as the "Beginning. Furthermore, it is called "Partial" because it posits both those who will attain Buddhahood and those who will not;
thus, it is designated as "partial. △ Second, the explanation of the meaning of the teaching.
What has been explained here is a broad discussion of *dharmalakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics), with little reference to *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).

That which is called "nature" (*tā*) is also merely a category of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), because it establishes the causes of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa based upon the eight consciousnesses and their various categories of meaning.

The Commentary states: "As for what was said regarding 'extensively discussing the characteristics of phenomena' (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) below, it refers to the Mahāyāna characteristics of phenomena, which number one hundred.

Specifically, there are eleven material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), eight mental phenomena (*cittadharma*), fifty-one mental concomitants (*caitasika*), twenty-four formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), and six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus, they total one hundred. This is in addition to the seventy-five [categories] of the preceding Hīnayāna."
In the middle [section], twenty-five are added. This means that seven are added for mental factors (*caitta*), because in the Hīnayāna there is only the single *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness).

Five are added for mental concomitants (*caittasika*). Ten are added for non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Three are added for unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). All these are as explained therein.

Regarding the commentary’s mention of "fewer and the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*): in the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* (Abhidharma) system, there are ninety-four categories of phenomena; however, since unconditioned phenomena belong to the category of "nature," only six are obtained [therein].
Therefore, it is merely called "nature" (dharmatā) because of its numerical [classification]. What is referred to as "nature" is itself a characteristic (lakṣaṇa) and a number.

Now, regarding the fact that unconditioned dharmas (asaṃskṛtadharma) are defined by the meaning of "dharma-nature," even though they are clearly determined and distinguished, the fact that there are six such numbers shows that although one speaks of their "nature," they too exist within the realm of names, characteristics, and numbers.
The sub-commentary (*śū*), starting from "based on the eight consciousnesses," refers to the Hīnayāna.

In the Dharma, the sixth consciousness is taken as the cause of defilement and purity. Now, in the Initial Teaching (Śāstra), it is held that *nirvāṇa* exists by depending upon the eighth consciousness;

thus it is said: "The realm (*dhātu*) existing from beginningless time is the equal support for all dharmas. From this arise the various realms of existence (*gati*) as well as the realization of *nirvāṇa*.
Here, "realm" (*dhātu*) has the sense of "cause," meaning the seeds and so forth. The Commentary states: "The various meanings..."
"Categories" (lei) refers to a summary of the many meanings within the Initial Teaching (shijiao). It is merely intended to avoid excessive prolixity in this commentary.
For a detailed understanding, one should consult the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Weishi lun) and the *Huayan xuantan*. △ Third, the Final Teaching (zhongjiao).
This section has two parts. First, the establishment of the name.
The Third: The Final Teaching of the Mahāyāna.

According to the *Chao*, this teaching contains explanations that were not fully exhausted in the preceding Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna; therefore, because these explanations are here brought to completion, it is called "Final.
If one follows the doctrinal classification of the master Jñānaprabha, this is precisely the third [teaching], the Non-characteristic Mahāyāna.
Regarding the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*): although the two teachings of the Sudden and the Perfect are also included within this meaning, they are only partially subsumed therein.
△ Second, the explanation of the text has two parts: first, the explanation of the names and meanings.
By emerging from the Middle Way, it reveals that those of fixed nature and icchantikas shall all become Buddhas; only then does it exhaustively expound the ultimate teaching of the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, it is called "final. Because it accords with the true principle, it is further named the "Teaching of Reality."
Commentary: From the passage "arising from the wondrous existence of the Middle Way" downward, it is because the true mark is free from marks;

since the wondrous existence of the Middle Way is neither form nor emptiness, delusive marks are fundamentally exhausted and true nature is fundamentally manifest. All sentient beings are originally Buddhas.
How could it be that those of the two vehicles with fixed natures, as well as the icchantikas who lack the nature for enlightenment, would not attain Buddhahood?

In the previous Initial Teaching (Śāstra), there was both attainment and non-attainment of Buddhahood; however, in this present teaching, it is permitted that all sentient beings shall ultimately attain Buddhahood.
Since this meaning surpasses the former, it is said: "This alone exhausts the ultimate discourse of the Mahāyāna," and is thus named [the Final Teaching].

This concludes the section [on the teaching]. Because it purely reveals the wondrous principle of the true aspect (*dharmatā*), it is further termed the "Teaching of Reality" (*shijiao*). △ Second, the explanation of the meaning of the teaching:

What is taught consists mostly of discourse on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and little regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*); even the "characteristics" mentioned therein ultimately converge back into the nature.
Because, by relying on the *tathāgatagarbha*, all categories of phenomena are established according to conditions.
[The *Chao*] states: "What is taught therein mostly discusses the *dharmatā*," because it exclusively reveals the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

As for what is called "phenomena" (*lakṣaṇa*), these also ultimately converge into the nature (*dhātu*); as it is said regarding the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*): "The five aggregates are themselves emptiness; emptiness is..."
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* states: "The five aggregates throughout the three periods of time are designated as the 'world';
their cessation is not the world; thus they are merely provisional names. It further says: "That which has contention is called saṃsāra; that which is without contention is called nirvāṇa."
"Samsara and nirvana—both are unattainable," and so forth. Furthermore, as it is said regarding the mind: "The mind is itself free from conceptualization.
Just so, although this sutra speaks of practicing the perfections such as generosity (*dānapāramitā*), all these ultimately converge upon the sublime practice that is free from signs;

thus, they are of the nature of *prajñā*. Therefore, it is said that even what is called "signs" ultimately returns to that very nature. This is because [the teachings] rely upon the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*).

Regarding the statement that "the *tathāgatagarbha* establishes various categories of meaning according to conditions": there are two senses in which the *tathāgatagarbha* establishes [phenomena] according to conditions.
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "First is the gate of the true suchness of mind (*citta-tathatā-mukha*); second is the gate of the arising and ceasing of mind (*citta-utpāda-nirodha-mukha*).
These two gates are both said to comprehensively encompass all phenomena. As for the arising and ceasing of mind, it is based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*. Therefore...
The mind that undergoes arising and ceasing has a basis, namely, the non-arising and non-ceasing. It is in union with arising and ceasing, being neither identical nor different.
All sentient beings are of one equal nature; both are established as True Suchness (tathatā) following conditions.

Since the dependent nature lacks inherent existence, it is itself the perfected nature. Because this single principle is uniform and level, it is said that the realm of sentient beings does not decrease, nor does the realm of Buddhas increase.

It does not increase, because such categories of meaning are vast, numerous, and inexhaustible. △ Fourth, the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao). This section has two parts. First, the establishment of the name:
"The fourth is the Sudden Teaching."

Commentary: Because the three teachings of the initial and final small vehicle mentioned previously are collectively termed "gradual," this present teaching—which is free from words and transcends all dependencies—is called "sudden" in contrast to those gradual teachings.
This is because "the sudden" does not establish the meaning of gradual progression. II.
Explanation of the Textual Meaning, in two parts: A. Explanation of the Meaning of the Name.
In sum, this does not depart from the characteristics of the teaching of the Dharma; it merely distinguishes true nature. When not a single thought arises, one is immediately named a Buddha.
Because there is no gradual progression, it is called "Sudden."
Commentary: When not a single thought arises, one is immediately called a Buddha. Because one encounters the Real at every point of contact, there is no sense of gradual progression;
thus, the name "Sudden" (Dun) is established. △ Second, explaining the meaning of the teaching.
The five dharmas and the three natures are both absent; the eight consciousnesses and the two forms of selflessness are both discarded. One censures the teachings and exhorts detachment;
one destroys appearances and extinguishes the mind, for all such categories of meaning are thus.

The Commentary states: First, name; second, appearance; third, false discrimination; fourth, correct wisdom; fifth, suchness. Regarding the three natures: first, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);

second, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); third, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). These are the three natures. Regarding the two kinds of selflessness: first, the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*); second, the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
As for the reproaching of teachings and the exhortation to depart from them: this is because the Dharma was transmitted from the West and does not establish [provisional] teachings.

Regarding the text: because it is "sealing mind with mind" and "sealing dharma with dharma," the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the principle of the two kinds of selflessness are all swept away, for they transcend the path of language.
Such categories of meaning are as extensively detailed in the subtle doctrines of various sutras such as the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Vajracchedikā*.
△ Fifth, the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). The text has two parts. First, the establishment [of the teaching].
Regarding the name "Five Perfect Teachings" (wǔ yuánjiào):

according to the *Jìyì* (Commentary), because the preceding [classification] established the name "Sudden" based on the "Gradual," and established the name "Gradual" based on the "Sudden," it now establishes [the Perfect Teaching] based on the "Gradual."
Regarding the term "sudden" (*dun*): it refers to the three teachings of the Initial [Hīnayāna], the Final [Mahāyāna], and the Small [Hīnayāna].

Because this Dharma cannot be demonstrated and because its verbal expressions and characteristics are quiescent, it is called "sudden. Regarding the establishment of the term "gradual" (*jian*) based on the sudden:
all sages and worthies possess distinctions based upon the unconditioned Dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); therefore, it is called "gradual. Thus, the sudden does not obstruct the gradual.

Because it follows the sequential order of gradual unfolding, the gradual does not obstruct the sudden; because it is perfectly accomplished in every instance, the sudden and gradual are mutually unimpeded.
By means of this, one enters the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong). Therefore, at this fifth stage, the name "Perfect Teaching" is established.
II. Explanation of the Textual Meaning, in two parts: 1. Explanation of the Meaning of the Name.
It encompasses the previous four [teachings] and is perfectly complete; thus it is named "Perfect" (Yuan). The *Chao* states:
"To encompass the previous four" refers to the four meanings of Initial, Final, Sudden, and Perfect.

Because these are subsumed within the Perfect, it is like the hundred rivers in the ocean, which share a single universal flavor; this is called being "perfectly complete. Therefore, there is perfect faith and perfect understanding.

Perfect cultivation, perfect practice, and perfect realization. Because the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, and the fruition penetrates to the perfection of the cause, it is given the name "perfect" (yuan).
△ Second, the explanation of the doctrinal meaning.

That which is taught is exclusively the inexhaustible Dharma-realm. Its ocean of nature is perfectly interfused; its dependent origination is unimpeded; its aspects are mutually identical and mutually inclusive;
like a net of Indra, they are layered upon one another; lords and attendants intersect with one another—because it is inexhaustible, inexhaustibly so.
△ Third, the names and meanings of the three summaries and five teachings.
The meanings of these aforementioned five teachings are explained in detail in the *Huayan Xuantan* (Profound Discussion of the Avataṃsaka); fearing prolixity, they are not cited here.

Regarding the phrase "fearing prolixity, they are not cited," this indicates that what is presented here is a summary, while the full meaning is found in the extensive treatises. △ Second, the classification and subsumption.
The "Returning" [to the source] has three parts. First is the primary attribution to that which is returned to.
This present sutra primarily belongs to the Final [Teaching], while also being accessible to the Sudden [Teaching]; its meaning encompasses both the Small Vehicle and the Initial [Teaching].
△ Second, citing scriptural evidence, which is divided into three parts.

First, proving the meaning of the Ultimate Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*). The text states: "The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. It further states: "If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
And it says: "The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata," and so forth.
This represents the perfect integration of phenomena and principle, the non-obstruction of the two truths, and the special manifestation of the Middle Way;

it is precisely the wondrous meaning of the "true reality of all dharmas" (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇa*) from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Furthermore, it is said that when the mind of faith is pure, one immediately gives birth to true reality; this subsumes the meaning of the Final Teaching (*paryantavāda*).
△ Second, the proof of the meaning of the Sudden Teaching.
It further states: "To be free from all marks is itself to be called a Buddha. This is the essential principle of the Sudden Teaching, which destroys marks and extinguishes the mind.
It further states: "By practicing all wholesome deeds through the four marks such as non-self, one immediately attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is also the meaning of the Sudden Teaching.
△ Third, proving the Initial Teaching to demonstrate the meaning of revealing the nature.

Furthermore, it is said: "Can one perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks? This question borrows from the perspective of the Hīnayāna—that phenomena exist externally to the mind—to probe the Venerable One;
thus, it accords with the meaning of the Lesser Teaching (Hīnayāna). The Venerable One, having grasped the intent, immediately refutes it by saying:
"One cannot perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. By refuting the marks to reveal the nature, he borrows the meaning of the Initial Teaching (Śūnyatāvāda).
Nevertheless, although this sutra employs the functions of both the Small and Initial Vehicles as provisional gateways, it subsumes them back into the source of the Final and Sudden Vehicles,
for it directly points to the One Vehicle, the non-dual Dharma.
△ Third, explaining away potential objections. Question:
Why is it not included within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao)? Answer: It belongs only to a small portion of the Perfect Teaching; thus, it is not explicitly presented as such.

For this reason, the Great Master Xianshou judged the *Avataṃsaka* to be the One Vehicle of the Perfect Teaching based on two meanings: first, as the "Teaching of Commonality" (Tongjiao) One Vehicle; [and second, as the "Teaching of Distinctness" (Biejiao) One Vehicle].

Regarding the vehicles, there are two types of One Vehicle: the One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching and the One Vehicle of the Distinct Teaching. The One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching is identical to the Sudden and the Final [teachings].

The One Vehicle of the Distinct Teaching is inconceivable. This present sutra is subsumed under the One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching of the Avataṃsaka, and is not subsumed under the One Vehicle of the Distinct Teaching.
△ Third, the explanation of the twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga*). This section has three parts. First, the enumeration of the names.

Regarding the "twelve divisions": 1. Sūtra (*sūtra*); 2. Verses (*geya*); 3. Prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*); 4. Independent Utterances (*udāna*); 5. Causes and Conditions (*nidāna*); 6. Unprompted Discourses (*itivṛttaka*);
7. Past Lives (*jātaka*); 8. Former Deeds (*vaipulya*); 9. Former Births (*adbhuta-dharma*); 10. Marvelous Events (*avadāna*); 11. ... [text fragment] ... 12. [Upadeśa].
The analogies and the twelve points of discussion.
II. Regarding their classification and affiliation:
this present sutra belongs to the category of the Eightfold Division (*aṣṭāṅga*). Since this sutra belongs to the Sūtra Piṭaka, is it not [the case that...]?
Because it is subsumed under the *sūtra* (discourses), it is spoken by the Venerable One in response to a request; thus, it is subsumed under the *nidāna* (causes and conditions).

Verses such as "Those who see me by means of form, or all conditioned phenomena," are subsumed under the *udāna* (inspired utterances). The account of King Kali cutting off [the Buddha's] limbs is subsumed under the *itivṛttaka* (past events).
That which the Tathāgata taught for those who have set out in the Mahāyāna is subsumed under the *vaipulya* (extensive teachings).
Because it is subsumed [within these categories]: the wisdom-eye I have attained since ancient times has never before heard such a sutra, for it is not something previously subsumed;
because it is subsumed under metaphors such as dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows;
because it is subsumed under formal discussion through the exchange of questions and answers between host and guest; and although within the text there is the past prediction of Dīpaṃkara...

The account of his having been a *kṣānti-rṣi* for five hundred lifetimes is subsumed solely under the category of *itivṛttaka* (Past Deeds), as it is not subsumed under *vyākaraṇa* (Prophecy) or *jātaka* (Birth Stories).
Furthermore, since there is no correspondence whatsoever between this and the meaning of the *geya* (Verses), it is not subsumed under that category either.
Therefore, among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it is subsumed exclusively within eight of them.
△ Third, the general conclusion.
The first section, "The Second Treasury: The Classification and Subsumption of the Teachings," is hereby completed.

Third, reconciling with other schools.
△ Second, explaining the text. This is divided into six parts. First, a general summary of the main intent:

Having already detailed this sutra, it belongs to the One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching (tóngjiào yīshèng). However, the One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching is the fundamental framework of all sutras.
This encompasses the fundamental source of the Tripitaka; therefore, it is a single, coherent whole from beginning to end, without distinction.

One should know that although the teachings are divided into five periods, they fundamentally do not differ. Starting with the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, followed by the Āgamas, then the Vaipulya, then the Prajñāpāramitā, and finally culminating in the profound mystery (the Huayan), these constitute the root.
△ Second, citing sutras to establish the proof. This section has six parts. First, citing Abhidharma treatises to clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Thus, the *Ahan Lun* (Abhidharma-śāstra) says: "There is no aging-and-death" refers to the emptiness of phenomena; "there is no one who ages-and-dies" refers to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
△ Second, citing the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Zhilun) to clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Furthermore, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "Within the Tripiṭaka, the emptiness of phenomena is explained as the Great Emptiness; within the Mahāyāna, the emptiness of the ten directions is explained as the Great Emptiness.
This demonstrates that the Lesser Vehicle already possesses two types of emptiness. Moreover, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says: "From the initial attainment of the Way..."
Up until the attainment of nirvana, he constantly preached the Prajñāpāramitā.
This is because, from beginning to end, the Prajñāpāramitā serves as the fundamental basis. △ Third, citing the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* to clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Contemplate the true mark of the body; contemplate the Buddha in the same way.
The commentary notes that the *Vimalakīrti* says: At that time, the World-Honored One asked Vimalakīrti, "Do you wish to see the Tathāgata?
By what means do you contemplate the Tathāgata? Vimalakīrti replied, "Just as I contemplate the true mark of my own body, so too do I contemplate the Buddha."
Nevertheless, as I contemplate the Tathāgata, he does not come from the past, nor does he go to the future, nor does he abide in the present.
I do not contemplate form, nor the suchness of form, nor the nature of form; I do not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor the suchness of consciousness.

The passage beginning with "not observing the nature of consciousness" (this selection of text and meaning refers to the fact that by contemplating the body of the five aggregates, one immediately realizes the wondrous principle of true reality, *tathatā*, and *prajñā*).
△ Fourth, citing the root sūtra to clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
This sutra states: "When the mind of faith is pure, one immediately gives rise to the mark of reality (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*)," and so forth;
because this is the meaning of *prajñā*, the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra) also explains that buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is named *prajñā*.
△ Fifth, citing the *Prajñāpāramitā* to clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Those who wish to attain the Śrāvaka vehicle should study the *Prajñāpāramitā*; those who wish to attain the Pratyekabuddha vehicle..."
One should study the *prajñāpāramitā*. Those who wish to attain the Bodhisattva Vehicle should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Thus, as the three animals cross the river, each describes it differently as clear or shallow; they divide the river to drink from it, and therein lie their thousandfold differences.

Therefore, while the Tathāgata’s Dharma accords with the capacities of beings and thus the teachings distinguish between vehicles (*yāna*), if one carefully traces back to the source, there is but a single Dharma.

The Commentary states: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says, "Desiring to attain the [fruit of] Śrāvaka," and so forth. This is because one enters the three vehicles by means of the water of Prajñā-wisdom.

Therefore, with inferior wisdom one attains the enlightenment of a Śrāvaka; with middling wisdom, the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha; and with superior wisdom, unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*).
This is why it is said that the three animals cross the river: first, a rabbit; second, a deer; and third, a horse. By means of the rabbit...
When a deer crosses the river, he says, "The water is too deep. When a horse crosses the river, he says, "The water is too shallow.
Thus it is said that each speaks of its own depth or shallowness; they divide the river and drink the water, for there are naturally a thousand differences.
It is said that in Western India there is a river named the Ganges, which is like the Qinhuai River here in this land. This refers to the individual gates of each person.
When drinking water from the mouth, the clear and the turbid are not equal, and the flavors differ; these are two metaphors. Water is a metaphor for *prajñā* (wisdom);
the nature of water is non-dual, yet the capacities [of beings] have depths and shallows, and their afflictions and evils are not the same.

Therefore, the Tathāgata’s Dharma descends according to the capacity of the individual, corresponding to the two preceding metaphors. Regarding both the Dharma and the appropriate capacity, if one carefully traces the source, there is but a single Dharma.
This means that the nature of the water of *prajñā* is without duality or distinction. △ Sixth, citing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
The Sūtra says: "In the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third, except for the skillful means taught by the Buddhas.
This Single Vehicle Dharma is precisely the Dharma of *prajñā*.
The Commentary states: It cites the *Lotus Sūtra*’s One Vehicle of the True Mark (śūnyatā), yet explains it through the differentiation of the Three Vehicles.

Now, the fundamental Dharma is directly revealed, for therein there are neither two nor three. If there were an explanation of three, it would merely be speech according to the intentions of others—a teaching of skillful means.
△ Third, explaining away obstacles and difficulties, in two parts: first, the objection.
Question: Since there is only the single dharma of Prajñā, why was the *Avataṃsaka* preached at the beginning and the *Nirvāṇa* proclaimed at the end?
II. Explaining and resolving the objection, divided into two parts. First: arising from the root to manifest the branches.

Answer: The *Avataṃsaka* is intended to directly reveal [the truth] to sentient beings of the supreme, highest faculties; however, as for those of middling and inferior capacities who have not yet been instructed, the One Buddha Vehicle is therefore explained by distinguishing it into three.
△ Second, returning the branches to the root.
Guiding him step by step with skillful means, he leads him into the Prajñāpāramitā, the Mahāyāna wisdom of emptiness. What was previously brought forth and received was what the son already knew.
Thus, at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the wisdom of emptiness (*prajñā*) was once again entrusted as the family inheritance.
Those of the three vehicles all received the prediction of Buddhahood, and the great treasure of the Dharma King arrived spontaneously.

As the derivative is brought back to the fundamental and flows into omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), one knows that if the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* were devoid of the dharma of *prajñā*, what would there be to entrust?
Commentary: "Gently guiding with persistent encouragement" refers to the period of the Āgamas, when the minor teachings on the causes and effects of devas and humans were extensively expounded;
by means of this gentle and persistent guidance, those lost in the stream of delusion were led to enter Nirvāṇa.

Second, "introducing them to the Prajñāpāramitā and the Mahāyāna wisdom of emptiness" refers to the assembly of the Vaipulya sūtras, where the Mahāyāna of Dharma-characteristics was discussed. Third, as for "that which was previously... [the text continues].

Regarding "receiving and disbursing": that which this son knows refers to the Tathāgata’s entrusting of the Dharma-wealth of the Prajñā-pāramitā and the wisdom of emptiness to Subhūti, Kāśyapa, Pūrṇa, and others, so as to transform all bodhisattvas; therefore, it is said, "that which this son knows.
Fourth, at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, he further entrusted the family inheritance of the Prajñā-pāramitā and the wisdom of emptiness [to Śāriputra]; although the Dharma...
Regarding the bestowal of the prediction of Buddhahood upon Huā:
it is by means of the Dharma of Prajñā that he is entrusted with it, for only then can he flow into all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Fifth, the conclusion below provides a summary and praise:

"Thus we know that if one lacks Prajñā, then even if one uses mind to seal mind and Dharma to accord with Dharma, one will certainly be unable to receive the prediction of Buddhahood. △ Fourth, the demonstration of Prajñā.
The entry into all phenomena consists of five sections. The first indicates that Prajñā is the meaning of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Thus, the dharma of Prajñā constitutes the One True Dharma-realm within the *Avataṃsaka*;
by practicing through various arts, one is led to enter the gateway of Prajñāpāramitā.
Commentary: Sudhana first approached Samantabhadra, who did not offer a single word of instruction (symbolizing that the male principle pervades all places).
He directed him instead to the youth Viśvāmitra, who sang the Dharani-gate of the forty-two letters, beginning with 'A' and ending with 'Ta,' thereby representing the Bodhisattva.
One enters the true path of Bodhi through the forty-two stages of the noble ones, because one practices them all in reliance upon the Dharma-gate of Prajñāpāramitā.
△ Second, pointing out that Prajñā is the meaning of the ultimate reality (dharmatā).
In all Mahāyāna sūtras, this refers to the Prajñā of the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).

As the Commentary states: "All the teachings of the Tathāgata throughout his lifetime are based upon the True Mark as their foundation; apart from this True Mark, there is no dharma that can be explained.
△ Third, pointing out that Prajñā is itself the nature of the Vajra.
In this sutra, it is the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*.
The commentary states that the sutra says: The Venerable One asked the Buddha, "How should we uphold this sutra?
The Buddha told Subhūti, "This sutra is named the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*. By this name, you should uphold it."
Uphold it. Why is this? The Buddha taught that the Prajñāpāramitā is, in its very nature, not the Prajñāpāramitā, and so forth.
(4) This points to the meaning of the Prajñā as the treasury of awakening.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is called the "Original Source Awakened Treasury" (*benyuan juezang*). Regarding this "Awakened Treasury," it is the meaning of *prajñā*.
The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "The 'Original Source' is the self-nature of *tathatā*; the 'Awakened Treasury' is the wisdom of *prajñā*.
Therefore, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says: "From the very beginning, the self-nature is fully endowed with all merits, namely..."
Because its own essence possesses the meaning of great wisdom-light; because it has the meaning of universally illuminating the dharma-realm;
because it has the meaning of true knowledge; because it has the meaning of the intrinsically pure mind; because it has the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity;

and because it has the meaning of being cool, unchanging, and sovereign—it is fully endowed with such qualities as exceed the sands of the Ganges, which are inseparable, uninterrupted, and non-different [from the essence].
Because the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas are fulfilled such that there is nothing lacking, he is called the Tathāgata;
he is also called the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata. The treatise further asks: "It was previously stated that the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) is equal and free from all marks;
why, then, is it said that its essence possesses distinctions, such as these various kinds of merit? The answer is: Although...
In reality, these various meanings of merit exist, yet they lack any characteristic of differentiation; they are equal in a single flavor, being nothing other than the one True Suchness (*tathatā*).
What is the meaning of this? Because it is non-conceptual and free from the marks of conceptualization, it is therefore non-dual.
△ Second, pointing out that Prajñā is itself the nature of Nirvāṇa. First, the formal presentation of the names and categories.
In *nirvāṇa*, it is the eternally abiding, wondrous nature; it is also the meaning of *prajñā*.
△ Second, citing scriptures to establish this proof:
Therefore, when the World-Honored One was about to enter the hidden radiance [of parinirvāṇa], he said: "By the power of my *mahāprajñā*, I have universally observed the triple world."
The various mountains, the great oceans, the vast earth, and all sentient beings—such as these three realms—are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature;
they are ultimately quiescent and equal to the characteristics of empty space.
Commentary: When the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, he suddenly revealed *samādhi* and *samāpatti* three times in succession.
Emerging from meditative concentration, he addressed the assembly, saying:

"By the power of my *mahāprajñā*, I have attained equality with empty space," thereby demonstrating how all Buddhas and Tathāgatas achieve enlightenment, turn the wheel of Dharma, and enter *nirvāṇa*.
The bowl and other such items are all accomplished through the power of *prajñā*. If *prajñā* lacked its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), what could serve as their foundation?
△ Fifth: Different Names, Identical Meaning.
Thus we know that although the names differ, the sublime intent is no different. Is this not because Prajñā is the foundation of all dharmas?
△ Sixth, the Sages and Worthies Rely on the Same [Foundation].
Therefore, it is that upon which the three classes of sages rely and that which is realized through the ten stages. All Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time rely upon Prajñā;
thus, those who attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi do so because they contemplate with a single essence the non-dual Dharma.
Commentary: Since Prajñā is the mother of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, how could those of the Three Stages of Worthies and the Ten Grounds not rely on this Dharma for their cultivation?
Therefore, the Three Stages of Worthies constitute the Prajñā of Understanding and Practice; the Ten Grounds constitute the Prajñā of Cultivation and Realization;
and the Buddhas constitute the Ultimate Prajñā. Thus, from cause to fruit, there is nothing that is not Prajñā.
If it is merely by the power of its nature. △ Third, the conclusion.
Thus ends the first section concerning the textual meaning of the remaining portions of the third assembly.

△ Section Four: The Three Vehicles and Their Recipients. Part One: The Preface.
Regarding the fourth, the capacities of those to be guided by this vehicle.

△ Second, the enumeration of chapters. This section has two parts. First, a general summary of the main intent, divided into five sections. First: the equality of the essence of sentient beings and Buddhas.

Since both things and self are without deficiency and are inherently possessed by all, the wisdom of *prajñā*—from the sages above to the commoners below—is equally rooted in the same source; its illuminating essence stands alone.
The Commentary states: An ancient worthy said, "Heaven and earth share my same age; the myriad things share my same substance.
Therefore, all sages and ordinary beings alike take the wisdom of prajñā-emptiness as their foundation. Thus it is said:

"Uniformly rooted and sharing the same source, the illuminating essence stands alone," for from the very beginning it has remained unchanging. △ Second, the distinction between delusion and awakening.
Those who are deluded sink into oblivion for eternal kalpas; those who awaken attain it in a single kṣaṇa.
Commentary: The deluded are sentient beings; the awakened are the Buddhas. Thus, they are firmly able to realize that their origin is the same source.
When delusion is fully understood, it is itself the truth; how could there be any difference between the ordinary being and the Buddha? △ Third, regarding "hearing and seeing forming seeds":

alas, because sentient beings are deluded and lack awakening, when they hear the teaching on the principle of non-arising, some are startled, some are doubtful, some believe, and some do not believe—all of these become the causal seeds for *prajñā*.
How much more so for those who believe, accept, uphold, and practice according to the teaching!
The practices and so forth proceed naturally and directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for there is no detour or deviation.
△ Fourth, [the text] investigates which capacity can enter.
Now, since this sutra is a teaching of a single lifetime, its beginning and end are of one flavor; it is not yet known for what kind of capacity it is intended.
And thus one is able to enter.
△ Fifth, the section on the enumeration of the capacities of the audience.

Although the Dharma is of a single flavor, the capacities of the audience are divided into ten types. The first five distinguish those who are not suitable vessels; the latter five manifest those for whom [the teaching] is intended.

△ Second, the correct explanation of the text, in two parts, each with five sections. In the first section, regarding the exclusion of those who lack the five capacities, there are two parts: first, the exclusion of those lacking faith as being unsuitable vessels;
second, the formal exclusion itself. Regarding the first: the formal exclusion.
First, those lacking faith are not vessels for the Dharma. Having heard the meaning of the emptiness of Prajñā, they fail to understand it and instead give rise to slander.
The *Chao* states: "The Buddha can deliver all sentient beings, yet he cannot deliver those who lack faith or those with whom he has no karmic affinity.

Thus, even though Chen Dong’s aged mother was born at the same time as the Buddha, she still did not accept his transformation; how much less so others? Therefore, it is said: "Those without [faith]..."

They lack the capacity for faith; they are unable to receive and hear the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Even if they were to hear it, they would not give rise to faith and understanding, but instead would produce slander.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Because of destroying the Dharma and lacking faith, they fall into the three evil realms.
I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter *nirvāṇa*. 2. Citing Scriptures to Prove the Meaning.

The subsequent scripture states: "If I were to explain it in full detail, some who hear it would have their minds become deranged, fall into doubt and lack faith, and consequently descend into the evil realms."

Commentary: "If I were to explain it in full" and so forth, serves to establish the meaning of their lack of faith. △ Second, distinguishing those who oppose the truth and are not vessels for the Dharma, in two parts:
first, the actual distinction;
second, those who oppose the truth and are not vessels. Relying on this sutra to seek fame and profit, they preach the Dharma with impurity and accumulate perverse goodness.
Therefore, the *Chao* states that below the section on "contradicting the truth," the mind-ground is not luminous; one relies solely on language and characters without seeking the true,
ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*), and preaches the Dharma merely out of a desire for fame, profit, and honor.

This is because the mind is not pure. Therefore, because the mind is pure, one does not seek profit or sustenance, even down to the level of a śrāmaṇera, in order to seek the truth—the First Noble Truth. This is what the Buddha taught.

If there is even the slightest bit of teaching the Dharma for the sake of profit, it is the teaching of Māra. Thus, it is said: "Because it gathers together false goodness. II. Citing Scriptures to Prove the Meaning.
The Sutra below states: "If the mind grasps at marks, one is immediately attached to the marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.
△ Third, distinguishing those who deviate from reality and are not vessels [for the Dharma], in two parts. First, the actual distinction.

Third: those who deviate from reality and lack the capacity [for the Dharma]. This refers to those who grasp at the literal meaning of the words; because the ultimate truth transcends the realm of ordinary cognition, it does not enter their minds.
Regarding the phrase "deviating from reality and lacking the capacity" in the *Chao*: they deviate from the true First Noble Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

The reason they contradict the true meaning is that such individuals rely exclusively on language and written characters, clinging to their own views and interpretations, thereby falling into the trap of the "trap and snare" (the means being mistaken for the end).
Therefore, one cannot transcend the limits of emotional cognition or escape the confines of dogmatic views; this is because the most ultimate and profound principles have not yet entered the mind.
△ Second, citing sutras and treatises as proof, in three parts: first, citing a treatise as proof.
Therefore, the Treatise states: "There are five kinds of faults in grasping the meaning according to the literal sound.

The *Chao* (Commentary) explains: Regarding "grasping the meaning according to the literal sound," an ancient master said, "To generate understanding merely by following the words is an enemy to the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
to deviate from a single word of the sutras is the teaching of Māra. As for the "five kinds of faults": first, incorrect understanding; second, the loss of courageous diligence.
Third, deceiving others; fourth, slandering the Buddha; fifth, disparaging the Dharma. Second, citing sutras to substantiate the meaning:
the text below states, "If one grasps at the characteristics of dharmas, one is immediately attached to the characteristics of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span."
△ Third, the exclusion of the three superior types of practitioners:
because the three superior types of ordinary, deluded beings are not suitable vessels.
△ Fourth, the two points on how those who are narrow-minded and inferior are not suitable vessels. First, the selection of the [proper] practitioner.

Fourth, those who are narrow-minded and inferior are not suitable vessels. This means that all followers of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) who have fallen into the pit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) do not enter [this teaching].
The *Yichao* (Commentary) states: "Regarding those who are narrow-minded and inferior and are not suitable vessels, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
'The great medicinal tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom cannot provide growth or benefit except in two places; namely, all followers of the two vehicles who have fallen into the unconditioned.'"
It is like a vast and deep pit for those sentient beings who have destroyed their roots of goodness and are unfit vessels, drowning in the waters of great false views and craving;
yet, even toward them, he never feels weary or abandons them. △ Second, citing scriptures to prove the meaning.

The subsequent text states: "If there are those who delight in inferior dharmas and are attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span, they will be unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sutra to others."
△ Section Five: Those Who Guard the Provisional Are Not Vessels (2). First, the formal exclusion of those who guard the provisional.

Regarding "those who guard the provisional are not vessels": this refers to those great beings of the provisional teaching who, throughout immeasurable kalpas, practice giving by sacrificing their bodies and lives three times each day, as well as those who fill the great trichiliocosm with the seven treasures.
Commentary: In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa says:
"I have observed that throughout the trichiliocosm, there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed where Śākyamuni Tathāgata has not sacrificed his body and life.

This demonstrates the inexhaustibility of internal giving; furthermore, by means of the seven treasures and other offerings, external giving is likewise unfailing. Thus, both internal and external [generosity] are extensively propagated.
The giving is immeasurable; that is to say, the excellence of the perfection of dāna (generosity) is beyond compare. △ Second, the provisional designation for those who are not vessels:

If they have not yet heard the Dharma of non-self in the Prajñāpāramitā, or if having heard it at some time, they do not believe, do not understand, do not comply with, and do not enter into it—such individuals are still provisionally designated as "bodhisattvas."

Commentary: Although one may practice extensive giving, they are still merely counted among the ranks of great beings (*mahāsattva*). If one lacks the two kinds of roots of goodness, this is what is called a "bodhisattva in name only.
First, those who have not yet heard the *prajñāpāramitā*; because they have not heard it, how could they understand non-self and the absence of phenomena?
Second, those who have already heard the *prajñāpāramitā*; although they have heard the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not believe in it; because they do not believe...

Therefore, they do not understand. Because they do not understand, they do not accord with it and do not enter into it; these are those who practice in a state of delusion and are of narrow and inferior capacity.

How could they transcend the fruits of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and five patiences (*kṣānti*)? In the latter five sections that clarify what is being done for [the sake of others], there are five parts.
First, the actual application for the sake of the capacities [of sentient beings]. Within this, first is the formal selection.
First, the primary purpose: This refers to the sudden and wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle. Originally, it is not something that can be received by those of inferior capacity.
The *Chao* states: "If the Dharma is great and the capacity small, there can be no accord; if the capacity is great and the Dharma small, there likewise can be no accord.
Therefore, only one with the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden can accord with the Perfect and Sudden Dharma and receive it. Second, citing scriptures to substantiate this meaning.

Three. First, for the sake of those with the capacity to resolve upon the Great Vehicle (mahācitta), the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata speaks for those who set forth the Great Vehicle; he speaks for those of the Supreme Vehicle.
Second, it is proven that this arises from possessing the vessel of the Dharma (dharmabhājana).
Furthermore, it says: "The Tathāgata fully knows that such persons possess the great vessel of the Dharma and have accomplished immeasurable, inconceivable merit.
Because such persons as these shall shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
△ Third, the proof that they have long planted roots of goodness.

It further says: "If there are those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, and are able to give rise to faith in these words and take them as true, you should know that such persons have already planted various roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable tens of millions of Buddhas."
△ Third, the concluding praise:

It is truly because one has entered the stage of the right-determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) over many lifetimes that, upon hearing the *prajñā* of words and letters, one immediately enters contemplative observation, giving rise to faith and realizing the truth of the eternal and constant.
Were it not for having extensively made offerings to Buddhas and possessed roots of goodness, how could such accomplishment be achieved?
Commentary: First, as long as the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) are not yet fulfilled, one is said to have not yet entered the stage of certainty (*niyatarāśi*).
Because the mind is not empty and quiescent amidst the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), one does not understand the wondrous purport of Prajñāpāramitā.

Consequently, one relies solely on faith in the cause and effect of the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*), personally attends upon Mahāyāna spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and plants various roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). By the power of such habitual cultivation (*vāsanā*), one has not yet entered the stage of certainty. Second—
Having already entered the stage of faith, he suddenly gave rise to the Great Mind. Thus, upon hearing the Dharma of Prajñā, his mind-ground was opened and unobstructed beneath a single word.
Regarding the objects of the six sense-fields, he became vast, penetrating, and pure; he fully realized that his own nature is fundamentally and originally the Buddha.
There is no need to seek it elsewhere; this is called entering the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Therefore, by listening to the *prajñā* of words and letters, one immediately enters contemplative observation and gives rise to faith, thereby realizing the true and eternal.

If it were not for the fact that [the practitioner] has, over many lifetimes, been in the presence of Buddhas and diligently cultivated precepts, concentration, wisdom, and so forth—possessing the power of the seeds of *prajñā* and various roots of goodness—the heart-ground would not yet have attained awakening. Now...
Furthermore, listen again: naturally, within the realms of sound and form, at every point of contact, there is perfect clarity; the essence shines forth, standing alone by itself.
△ Second, the combined [explanation], divided into three parts. First, the formal selection.
The second is that which serves both purposes. This refers to those who, out of reverence and faith, hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite this Dharma;

although they have not yet attained realization, they are able to develop faith and inclination, thereby establishing the seed [of enlightenment], just as when a person consumes a small amount of *vajra* (diamond).

Commentary: Question: One must grasp the essential meaning of the sutras and attain spiritual realization through the mind before one can truly believe and turn toward them to form the seed [of enlightenment].
Now, since you merely believe in the words and letters, how can this possibly form the seed? Answer: Although one hears the words and letters...

That which constitutes the seed through faith and orientation toward *prajñā* is the untainted (*anāsrava*) sublime Dharma. It permeates and enters the tainted (*sāsrava*) mind of the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Whether through reverence, faith, upholding, recitation, or making offerings—each of these is the power of the Dharma of *prajñā* acting with intimacy and strength.
Because it has now permeated and entered the tainted mind of this present life, it continues until the causes are perfected.
When the fruit ripens, it immediately becomes the seed of the untainted (*anāsrava*). It is like a person who eats a small amount of *vajra* (diamond/thunderbolt);
"and so forth" refers to the remaining passages. Thus, the Great Being Samantabhadra addressed the Bodhisattvas regarding the Tathāgata-nature, saying:
"Just as when a person eats a small amount of *vajra*, it will inevitably pierce through the body and emerge from the outside. Why is this? Because the *vajra*..."
Because it dwells together with the physical body, it is likewise for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
if they hear the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas, they must ultimately pierce through the entire conditioned body to reach the unconditioned ground of omniscience.
Therefore, it is said that the "diamond-seed enters the Tathāgatagarbha," and so forth. △ Second, citing the sutra.
This is the proof of the meaning.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Even those who give rise to pure faith for a single thought-moment—the Tathāgata fully knows them and fully sees them," and so forth.
Because these sentient beings obtain such immeasurable merits, although they do not understand it now, they will certainly enter [the path] hereafter.
Commentary: There are two kinds of pure faith (*śraddhā*). First, one who in previous lives practiced giving and precepts extensively but heard little of the Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā;
